Racks and Cabinets: Anchoring, Clearances, Cable Management

Unit 3: Pathways and Spaces. Lesson 12 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

The rack arrives on a pallet and the crew wants it standing before lunch. Standing is not the same as secure. A rack holds hundreds of pounds of equipment and the cables that feed it, and it is the one thing in the room that can hurt someone if it falls.

Types

A two-post rack (also called a relay rack) holds light equipment and patch panels. A four-post rack or cabinet carries heavy equipment and gives better cable management. A wall mount serves small zones and needs a wall that can carry the full load. Equipment screws use M5, M6, 10-32, or 12-24 threads, with star washers for bonding.

Sizes

Item                 Standard
Width                483 mm (19 in); 584 mm (23 in) for service providers
Height               2.1 m (7 ft) normal
One rack unit (U)    about 45 mm (1.75 in) of vertical space

Anchoring and bracing

  • Bolt a floor rack to the floor with expansion anchors, flat washers, and lock washers.
  • Brace the top to the wall, a tray, or a ladder rack. Seismic bracing is whatever the AHJ requires.
  • A wall-mounted rack goes on lag bolts and washers into the plywood.

Clearances

Use double-sided racks and keep the front and the rear accessible. A rack pushed against a wall cannot be serviced. Plan the aisle so equipment can be moved in and out.

Cable management

Vertical managers run at the sides, and horizontal managers sit by each patch panel. Leave room for cord slack. D-rings are fine for small bundles and cross-connect jumpers, but they never replace a ladder rack. Secure power strips to the rack and plug them into the dedicated outlets.

Bonding

Every rack is bonded to the busbar with its own conductor. Never daisy-chain.

Tip: set the rack's hole pattern by the first piece of equipment, then do not move it after the cables are in.
Exam tip: anchor the rack to the floor, brace the top, and keep both the front and the rear accessible.
Remember
Anchor to the floor, brace the top, keep front and rear clear, manage cables with vertical and horizontal managers, and bond every rack.
Deeper explanation

Racks and Cabinets: Anchoring, Clearances, Cable Management, explained slowly

Sizing the rack for a 96-outlet floor

A rack is a stack of rack units, and every piece of equipment takes a number of them. One rack unit (1 U) is about 45 mm (1.75 in).

Item                                 Rack units
Four 24-port patch panels            4 U
Four horizontal cable managers       4 U
Switch (one per 48 ports)            2 x 1 U = 2 U
Backbone fiber panel                 1 U
Power strip, rear rail               0 U or 1 U
Total used                           11 U

Eleven rack units is 11 x 45 mm, which is about 495 mm (11 x 1.75 in, which is 19.25 in). A 2.1 m (7 ft) rack has far more space, so this leaves growth room. Never fill a rack to the top on day one.

Anchoring and bracing, in order

  1. Mark the footprint on the floor and drill for expansion anchors.
  2. Set the rack, add flat washers and lock washers, and tighten the anchors.
  3. Brace the top to the wall, a tray, or a ladder rack so the rack cannot tip.
  4. Apply any seismic bracing the AHJ requires.
  5. Bond the rack with its own conductor to the busbar.
Rack type        Best use                               Watch for
Two-post         patch panels, light equipment          tipping if overloaded
Four-post        heavy equipment                        weight; anchors
Cabinet          lockable, enclosed equipment           airflow and power
Wall mount       small zones and TEs                    wall must carry the load

Clearances

Use double-sided racks and keep both the front and the rear accessible. If no distance is specified, plan at least 1 m (3.28 ft) around and between equipment. A rack tight against a wall cannot be serviced.

Cable management

Vertical managers sit on the sides and carry the bundles up from the pathway. Horizontal managers go by each patch panel and hold the cords. D-rings are fine for small bundles and cross-connect jumpers, but a bundle of many cables needs a ladder rack. Leave cord slack and a gentle bend, never a tight loop.

Equipment fasteners

Use M5, M6, 10-32, or 12-24 threads to match the equipment, with star washers for bonding. A mixed bag of screws strips the threads.

Remember: anchor, brace, bond, and keep front and rear open.
